paragraphs: §1 — The "image and likeness" prooftext: the Angel who resembles humankind is the Creator of Adam

We have already reported his doctrine in the first Maqala, and we add here the mention of his prooftext. Among that which he adduced as a ground is the saying of Scripture [Gen 1:27] בבראש' א', כז' ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו וג' ("and God created the human being in His image" etc.). [He argued] that the pre-eternal Creator (al-Bārī al-qadīm) cannot have any likeness, nor any similitude, nor any form that is beheld; yet He has informed that He created the human being in His [own] form and likeness. And we have found that among the angels there are those who resemble human beings, since it says [Ezek 1:10] ביחז' א', י' ודמות פניהם פני אדם וג' ("and the likeness of their faces was the face of a human" etc.); and likewise [Gen 18:2] בבראש' יח', ב' וישא עיניו וירא והנה שלשה אנשים נצבים וג' ("and he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing" etc.), and they are angels beyond doubt; and it also says [Dan 9:21] בדנ' ט', כא' והאיש גבריאל אשר ראיתי וג' ("and the man Gabriel, whom I had seen" etc.). So from this we have come to know that the one who said [Gen 1:26] בבראש' א', כו' נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו ("let us make a human in our image, after our likeness") is the Angel who resembles human beings, and that he is the one of whom it is said [Gen 1:27] ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו וג' ("and God created the human being in His image" etc.). And he corroborated that also by His saying [Gen 3:22] בבראש' ג', כב' הן האדם היה כאחד ממנו ("behold, the human being has become like one of us").

: The opening prooftext is the same Gen 1:26-27 anthropomorphism-text that occupied Bab 6 §2 against the Christians — but turned to a wholly different purpose. Benjamin's logic: God can have no beheld "form," yet Adam is made "in His image"; and since some angels are described in human form (Ezek 1:10 "the face of a human"; the "three men" of Gen 18:2; Gabriel "the man" of Dan 9:21), the "image" in which Adam is made must be an angel's image — so the "let us make" of Gen 1:26 is spoken by the creating Angel, and "behold, the human has become like one of us" (Gen 3:22) confirms a plurality of angelic makers. Q reproduces the argument neutrally here; the refutation (the figurative reading of ṣelem / demut as "the form of an act, not of a body," already established in Maqala II and recalled in Bab 6 §2) is deferred to Bab 20 §5. Note that the demiurgic-angel doctrine and the Christian Trinitarian reading exploit the same plural-and-image verses, which is why Q's eventual refutation can be common to both.
§2 — The Angel as the one who multiplies and blesses the seed (Hagar; the Binding)

2. And they also adduced as a ground the saying of Scripture concerning Hagar [Gen 16:10] בבראש' טז', י' ויאמר לה מלאך יי הרבה ארבה את זרעך וג' ("and the angel of YHWH said to her, 'I will greatly multiply your seed'" etc.). So he informed that the Angel is the one who multiplies her seed; and he multiplies her seed only by creating them. And the like of that is in the story [Gen 22:1] בבראש' כב', א' והאלהים נסה את אברהם ("and God tested Abraham"), for it says [Gen 22:11] בבראש' כב', יא' ויקרא אליו מלאך יי מן השמים וג' ("and the angel of YHWH called to him from heaven" etc.), and that Angel says to him [Gen 22:17] בבראש' כב', יז' כי ברך אברכך והרבה ארבה את זרעך וג' ("for I will surely bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed" etc.), and it also says [Gen 22:18] בבראש' כב', יח' אשר שמעת בקולי ("because you obeyed my voice"). So he informed that the Angel is the one who blesses him, and is the one who multiplies his seed, and is the one who commands him, and that Abraham accepted his command.

: The second prooftext-cluster: the "angel of YHWH" (malʾakh YHWH) who, in the Hagar and ʿAqedah narratives, speaks in the first person as the one who blesses, multiplies, and commands. Benjamin's inference is that multiplying the seed is an act of creation ("he multiplies her seed only by creating them"), so the Angel is a creator; and the Angel commands and is obeyed as God is. The verses are exactly those where the malʾakh YHWH / malʾakh ha-Elohim alternation with the divine name has long invited a hypostatic or intermediary reading; Benjamin reads the intermediary as his demiurgic Angel.
§3 — The "three men" of Mamre: the chief of the three is the delegated Creator of all (Sodom)

3. And they also adduced as a ground His saying [Gen 18:1-3] בבראש' יח', א' [א'] וירא אליו יי באלני ממרא וג' [ב'] וישא עיניו וירא והנה שלשה אנשים וג' ("and YHWH appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre" etc.; "and he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men" etc.), and his saying there [Gen 18:3] [ג'] אם נא מצאתי חן בעיניך ("if now I have found favor in your eyes"); and that he directed the address to one of them, the one who is the chief (al-raʾīs) — and he is the one whom they alleged the Creator created alone (faqaṭ) and to whom He delegated (fawwaḍa) the creation of the whole world and the origination of all that comes to be. And he is the one of whom it is said [Gen 19:24] שם' יט' כד' [כד'] ויי המטיר על סדום ועל עמרה גפרית ואש וג' ("and YHWH rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire" etc.), and he is the one who said [Gen 19:21] שם' כא' [כא'] לבלתי הָפְכְּךָ את העיר אשר דברת ("that I should not overthrow the city of which you have spoken").

: The Mamre theophany (Gen 18) is the structural center of the doctrine. Of the "three men," the chief (al-raʾīs) — addressed by Abraham as adonai ("my lord," Gen 18:3) — is identified with the single Angel whom God created and to whom He delegated (fawwaḍa) the entire work of creation and providence. The delegation-verb fawwaḍa is the doctrine's keyword (it recurs in Bab 20's refutation, §3-4). The chief-angel is then read as the YHWH who destroys Sodom (Gen 19:24) and who entertains Abraham's plea over the city (Gen 19:21) — i.e., the demiurge is the agent throughout the Genesis theophanies.
§4 — Jacob's ladder, Laban's dream, and the bush: the Angel is "the God of Abraham"

4. And they adduced as a ground His saying concerning Jacob [Gen 28:12] בבראש' כח', יב' [יב'] ויחלם והנה סלם מצב ארצה ("and he dreamed, and behold, a ladder set up on the earth"), and his saying [Gen 28:13] שם' יג' [יג'] והנה יי נצב עליו ויאמר אני יי אלהי אברהם וג' ("and behold, YHWH stood over it and said, 'I am YHWH, the God of Abraham'" etc.). Then it says in the story of Laban [Gen 31:11] שם' לא' יא' [יא'] ויאמר אלי מלאך האלהים בחלום יעקב ("and the angel of God said to me in a dream, [O] Jacob"), and it says [Gen 31:13] שם' לא' יג' [יג'] אנכי האל בית אל אשר משחת שם מצבה אשר נדרת לי ("I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me"). So know from this that the Angel is the one who said to him "I am the God of Bethel" etc., and that it was to that Angel that he made that vow. And the like of that is His saying concerning Moses (may his memory be for a blessing) [Exod 3:2] בשמות ג' ב' [ב'] וירא מלאך יי אליו בלבת אש ("and the angel of YHWH appeared to him in a flame of fire"), and his saying [Exod 3:6] שם' ו' [ו'] ויאמר אנכי אלהי אביך ("and he said, 'I am the God of your father'"). So he informed that the Angel who appeared to him in the fire of the bush is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And this, in their view, is of the utmost cogency (fī ghāyat al-taʾkīd).

: The most weighty cluster ("of the utmost cogency," in the doctrine's own estimation): the verses where an angel speaks and is then identified, in the first person, as God. At the ladder, YHWH says "I am the God of Abraham" (Gen 28:13); in Jacob's recollection to his wives the speaker is "the angel of God" who says "I am the God of Bethel" (Gen 31:11, 13); at the burning bush "the angel of YHWH" appears and then says "I am the God of your father" (Exod 3:2, 6). Benjamin's inference: the being called "angel" and the being called "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" are one and the same — hence the patriarchal "God" is the created Angel. This is the angelological counterpart of the Christian exploitation of the malʾakh YHWH texts (cf. Bab 6 §3 on the aṣḥābunā reading of YHWH-as-speaker); Q's refutation (Bab 20 §5) will be that the prophets and angels routinely ascribe to themselves, in the surface of the speech, what in reality belongs to God.
§5 — The redeeming Angel, the Angel "sent before you," and the Angel of the Presence

5. And they also adduced as a ground the saying of Jacob [Gen 48:16] בבראש' מח' טז' [טז'] המלאך הגאל אתי מכל רע וג' ("the Angel who redeemed me from all evil" etc.), and the saying of God to Moses [Exod 23:20] בשמות כג' כ' [כ'] הנה אנכי שלח מלאך לפניך וג' ("behold, I send an angel before you" etc.), and the saying of Isaiah [Isa 63:9] ישעיהו סג' ט' [ט'] ומלאך פניו הושיעם ("and the angel of His presence saved them"), and the saying of David [Ps 35:5] בתהל' לה' ה' [ה'] ומלאך יי דוחה ("and the angel of YHWH driving [them]"), and his saying [Ps 35:6] שם' ו' [ו'] ומלאך יי רדפם ("and the angel of YHWH pursuing them"). So this is one kind (ḍarb wāḥid) of that which they adduce as a ground.

: A further class of proof: verses in which an angel performs the saving and judging acts elsewhere ascribed to God — the redeeming Angel of Jacob's blessing (Gen 48:16), the guardian Angel "sent before you" in the wilderness (Exod 23:20), the "angel of His presence" who saves (Isa 63:9), and the avenging "angel of YHWH" of Ps 35:5-6. Q closes the section by labeling all the foregoing (§§1-5) "one kind" (ḍarb wāḥid) of prooftext — the kind that infers the demiurgic Angel from passages where an angel acts as God — and proceeds in §6 to a second, distinct kind. Q's eventual reply (Bab 20 §6) concedes the premise but denies the inference: God does indeed send His angels to save and to destroy, just as He works such acts at the hands of human prophets — which establishes agency, not demiurgy.
§6 — A second kind of prooftext: "great above all gods" makes the Angel greatest among the angels

6. And they have another kind of prooftext, and that is of the genus of the saying of Jethro [Exod 18:11] יתרו בשמות יח' יא' [יא'] עתה ידעתי כי גדול יי מכל האלהים ("now I know that YHWH is greater than all the gods"). They said: he did not intend by this saying that the first Creator is greater than the rest of the gods that are the idols — since it is not admissible that a thing be compared or related to that from which it is at the utmost remove, but rather a thing is related and compared only to what is near it. So by that saying he intended only that this Angel, who created the world and who is the one who delivered them from Egypt, is greater and mightier than the rest of the angels. And the like is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him) [Deut 3:24] דבר' ג', כ"ד מי אל בשמים ובארץ אשר יעשה כמעשיך ("what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do according to Your deeds"), and his saying [Exod 15:11] בשמות ט"ו, י"א מי כמכה באלם יי ("who is like You among the gods, O YHWH"), and the saying of David (mercy be upon him) [Ps 135:5] בתהל' קל"ה, ה' כי אני ידעתי כי גדול יי ואדנינו מכל אלהים ("for I know that YHWH is great, and that our Lord is above all gods"), and his saying [Ps 86:8] בשם' פ"ו, ח' אין כמוך באלהים יי ואין כמעשיך ("there is none like You among the gods, O YHWH, and there are no works like Yours"), and his saying [Ps 97:9] בשם' צ"ז, ט' כי אתה יי עליון על כל הארץ ("for You, YHWH, are most high above all the earth"), and his saying [Ps 89:7] בשם' פ"ט, ז' כי מי בשחק יערך ליי ("for who in the sky can be compared to YHWH").

: The second class of prooftext is the comparative/superlative one: verses that call God "great above all gods" (Exod 18:11; cf. Deut 3:24; Exod 15:11; Pss 135:5, 86:8, 97:9, 89:7). The argument rests on a logical premise about comparison: a thing can only be meaningfully compared (yunqās / yuḍāf) to what is near its own kind, never to what is infinitely remote from it. So "YHWH is greater than all the gods" cannot mean the transcendent Creator exceeds mere idols (an incommensurable comparison); it must mean that this Angel — the world's creator and Israel's deliverer from Egypt — is the greatest among the angels, his peers. The comparison-premise is the load-bearing inference; Q's refutation (Bab 20 §7) will turn it back on the doctrine itself (if the Angel is the creator of the whole world, including the idols' raw matter, then he cannot be compared to idols either) and will gloss the verses as prophetic expressions of wonder at the worshippers' folly, not real comparisons.
§7 — Summary of the sources of the doctrine, and a rational (non-scriptural) variant

7. This, then, is what we have set out — part of it from the doctrine of Benjamin, part of it related to us concerning a group of his followers (aṣḥābihi), and part of it which we [ourselves] saw to be of the genus of what they adduce as a ground. We have mentioned it so that nothing in which they have a foothold (ʿalqa) should remain to them.

As for one of those whom we met among those who incline to this doctrine, he sought to indicate it by way of reason (min al-maʿqūl): he alleged that things are distinguished, and one is separated off from another, only by [essential] differentiae (fuṣūl) subsisting in them; and that the differentia by which the angels are separated off from human beings is the origination of bodies (ikhtirāʿ al-ajsām) — whence it is established that the originator of bodies is an angel.

: Q's closing remarks are methodologically candid: he distinguishes three sources for the catalogue he has assembled — (a) Benjamin's own stated doctrine, (b) what was reported to him about a group of Benjamin's followers, and (c) prooftexts Q himself supplied as being "of the same genus." His stated motive — "so that nothing in which they have a foothold (ʿalqa) should remain to them" — is the exhaustive-catalogue method he announced for the Christian polemic (the ẓannū anna lahum fīhi ʿalqa of the Bab 6 heading): he will not leave the strongest form of the opposing case unstated. The appended rational argument is distinct from all the scriptural ones: a quasi-philosophical claim that species are constituted by essential differentiae (fuṣūl), and that the differentia separating angels from humans is precisely the power to originate bodies (ikhtirāʿ al-ajsām) — so the world's body-maker is an angel. Q singles this out because it does not depend on exegesis at all, and he opens Bab 20 by demolishing it first (Bab 20 §1: the inference is built on an unconceded premise — that origination is the only differentia between angels and humans, when in fact many other differentiae distinguish them). The Arabic file for this bab ends mid-sentence within §6; the completion of §6 and the whole of §7 are recovered from the head of the Bab 20 file (Nemoy p178), before the al-bāb al-ʿishrīn heading.

- The bab's subject and the figure of Benjamin. The heading is fī qawl Binyāmīn fī al-malʾak — "on the doctrine of Benjamin concerning the Angel." The Benjamin in question is Binyāmīn al-Nahāwandī, the prominent early-9th-century Karaite jurist-exegete of Persia, to whom Q (here and in Maqala I, to which §7 back-refers) attributes a demiurgic-angel theology: the transcendent first Creator created a single exalted Angel and delegated (fawwaḍa) to it the making of the cosmos and the governance of events, so that the biblical YHWH who acts in the world is in fact this created Angel. The doctrine is plainly a response to anthropomorphism — its motive (stated in §1) is to keep the wholly transcendent Creator free of any "form that is beheld" by interposing a created intermediary — and it has obvious structural affinities both with the demiurge of late-antique Platonism/gnosticism and with the Logos/Metatron speculations of the period.

- A purely expository bab; the refutation is Bab 20. Unlike the catalogue-and-refute babs (5-6, 8), Bab 19 is only the iḥtijāj — the marshalling of the opposing case — with the radd held over entirely to Bab 20. This is the same two-bab architecture Q used for the Christian polemic (Bab 5 catalogue → Bab 6 refutation). Translating Bab 19 in isolation therefore yields an unrebutted statement of the angel-doctrine; the footnotes here flag, for each section, where Bab 20 takes up the reply, but the translation itself does not editorialize against the doctrine, faithfully preserving Q's neutral expository voice ("they adduced as a ground," "he alleged").

- The two "kinds" (ḍarb) of prooftext. Q explicitly structures the scriptural case into two ḍarb: (1) §§1-5, the verses where an angel acts as / speaks as God (the image-verses, the malʾakh YHWH of the patriarchal and Mosaic theophanies, the redeeming/avenging angels) — inferring demiurgy from agency; and (2) §6, the comparative verses ("greater than all gods"), inferring that the Angel is first among the angels from the logic that comparison presupposes commensurability. §7 then adds a third, non-scriptural register: a rational (maʿqūl) argument from essential differentiae. Recognizing this tripartite structure is essential to seeing how Bab 20's refutation is organized (it answers the rational argument first, then the two scriptural kinds).

- Shared prooftexts with the Christian polemic. Almost every verse Benjamin deploys here (Gen 1:26-27; the "three men" of Gen 18; the malʾakh YHWH texts; the "greater than all gods" verses) was also a Christian Trinitarian/Christological prooftext catalogued in Bab 5 and answered in Bab 6. This is not coincidence: both the demiurgic-angel doctrine and Christian intermediary-theology exploit the same hypostasis-suggesting features of the Hebrew text (the plural naʿaseh, the image-language, the malʾakh YHWH alternation with the Tetragrammaton). Q's philological refutations in Bab 6 (the figurative reading of ṣelem/demut; the prophets' habit of ascribing to themselves what belongs to God) are therefore largely transferable to Bab 20 — and Q in §1 explicitly recalls the Maqala II treatment of be-tzalmenu ki-demutenu that he will reuse.

- Key technical terms. fawwaḍa ("to delegate") is the doctrine's signature verb (the Creator delegates world-making to the Angel) and recurs as the target of Bab 20 §§3-4. ikhtirāʿ al-ajsām ("the origination of bodies") is the rational argument's claimed angelic differentia (§7). al-raʾīs ("the chief," §3) is the chief of the Mamre triad identified with the demiurge. ʿalqa ("foothold, attachment-point," §7) is the same polemical term as in the Bab 6 heading (mā ẓannū anna lahum fīhi ʿalqa) — Q's word for the residual handhold an opponent might claim. al-fuṣūl ("essential differentiae," §7) is the Porphyrian/logical term for species-constituting differences.

- OCR / textual note. The Hebrew citations in the merged source are the multimodal re-OCR readings; the diff-report (104 disagreements, all `letters_differ: true`) shows the Kraken column to be heavily garbled (e.g. Kraken `נששה אדם` / `בעלמנו כדמאננ` vs. multimodal `נעשה אדם` / `בצלמנו כדמותנו`), and the multimodal readings — which agree with MT — have been adopted throughout. No genuine lacunae remain in the span; the only "missing" runs in the Kraken column correspond to text the multimodal pass recovered in full. The single text-critical point worth flagging for the edition is that Q's verse-pointer for Isa 63:9 is given as ט' ("9"), correct; and that the Ps 35:5-6 pair is cited with ומלאך יי דוחה / ומלאך יי רדפם, where MT reads doḥeh / rodfam — Q's consonantal text matches MT.

- For Benjamin al-Nahāwandī's life, works, and angelology: Q's own Anwār Maqala I account of the Karaite sects (to which §7 explicitly back-refers); Leon Nemoy, "Al-Qirqisānī's Account of the Jewish Sects," HUCA 7 (1930), esp. the section on Benjamin; and the entries in Daniel Frank, Search Scripture Well (2004), and Meira Polliack (ed.), Karaite Judaism: A Guide to its History and Literary Sources (2003). - For the demiurgic-angel / created-mediator idea in its late-antique and Jewish context (the Logos, Metatron/"lesser YHWH," and angel-of-the-Lord speculations Benjamin's doctrine resembles): Daniel Boyarin, "Two Powers in Heaven; or, The Making of a Heresy," and Alan Segal, Two Powers in Heaven (1977); Peter Schäfer, The Origins of Jewish Mysticism (2009) on Metatron. - For the malʾakh YHWH / angel-of-the-Lord exegetical problem these verses raise (Gen 16, 18-19, 22; Exod 3, 23; Isa 63): the standard treatments in the Karaite and Rabbanite Genesis-Exodus commentaries; cf. Q's parallel use of the same verses (read as YHWH-as-speaker) in Bab 6 §3. - For the refutation that answers this bab: Bab 20 of this Maqala (fī al-radd ʿalayhim), which takes up the rational argument of §7 first (Bab 20 §1), then the delegation-doctrine (§§2-4), then the scriptural prooftexts of §§1-6 (§§5-7), reusing the figurative-language and prophetic-ascription arguments of Bab 6. - For the Bahshamī background to Q's eventual refutation (the impossibility of a created creator; fawwaḍa and secondary causation): ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī and Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa on al-tawḥīd and on the denial of intermediary creators.
